issues.item: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: For a man-made disaster trauma in a 58-year-old forensic analyst, this item is only coherent if there was a significant physical injury. The rest of the selected profile does not support an injury-based presentation: the threat items emphasize environmental danger and vigilance (limited safe places, loud sounds, unfamiliar places), while the other appraisals are about coping failure and loss of capability rather than concrete bodily injury. With no memory or strategy items to anchor a physical-injury narrative, this appraisal stands out as clinically hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
issues.explanation: The profile is not coherent with the supplied cognitive formulation because all cross-node edges are inactive, which implies these components should not appear as tightly linked aspects of one maintaining pattern. However, the Threat items and Negative Appraisal items are strongly conceptually connected: perceiving the world as dangerous maps directly onto restricted safety zones and avoidance of unfamiliar places, creating an active Threat–Negative Appraisal linkage that contradicts the formulation.

issues.item: Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
issues.explanation: Within the selected nodes, the content clusters into a classic mutually reinforcing danger/coping pattern rather than isolated components. 'World is a dangerous place' coheres directly with hypervigilance to sounds and avoidance of unfamiliar places, while 'Bad Coper' and 'No longer capable' reflect generalized post-trauma self-evaluation likely tied to the same threat response. With no active edges anywhere in the formulation, this degree of integration is inconsistent.

issues.item: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
issues.explanation: The formulation specifies no active edges, so the selected nodes should function as relatively isolated components rather than implying a tight linked syndrome. Here the Threat items and Negative Appraisal items form a classic connected PTSD pattern: danger-focused hypervigilance/startle and avoidance are closely mirrored by broad beliefs that the world is dangerous and that the self is incapable. This actively implies strong Threat↔Negative Appraisal linkage, which contradicts the fully disconnected formulation.

issues.item: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
issues.explanation: Within Threat, the items are coherent with each other, and within Negative Appraisals the items are also coherent. The problem is cross-node/formulation consistency: the profile presents mutually reinforcing danger sensitivity and negative self/world beliefs despite all edges being inactive.

vignette: Rafael had spent two decades trusting his training to read the quiet, methodical language of evidence. That certainty fractured the afternoon the regional logistics hub on the city’s eastern edge ruptured. He had arrived to document compromised structural supports when a secondary detonation tore through the facility. The world did not fade to black; it split into screaming metal and blinding heat. He remembered the sudden, violent shift in air pressure that threw him against a concrete pillar, the deafening collapse of overhead catwalks, and the terrifying, unpredictable rhythm of burning gases swallowing the corridor. He had crawled through smoke and twisted rebar to reach the street, his breath ragged, his hands shaking uncontrollably as sirens finally pierced the chaos. When the smoke cleared, he had walked away, but the ground beneath him felt permanently unstable. In the months that followed, his physiology refused to stand down. Even in his quiet kitchen, his body felt constantly tense and ready to react to danger, leaving him lying awake with shoulders braced and muscles coiled. A dropped pan or a car backfiring would send his heart hammering, his head snapping toward the noise before he could stop himself. He caught himself jumpy and easily startled during ordinary conversations, certain that his nervous system had broken beyond repair. What frightened him most was the conclusion he kept drawing about himself: his reactions since the event showed that he was a lousy coper. He had come to believe he was no longer capable of doing the things that defined him, particularly the calm, methodical site assessments that had anchored his career. The meticulous patience required to process a scene felt like a foreign language now. Consequently, he stopped driving to new districts. He could no longer tolerate stepping into unfamiliar places because he could not assess the danger, so he began routing his commute through the exact same three streets he had used for years. This avoidance bled directly into his daily work. At the county forensic processing center where he now reviewed only archival case files, the sudden ring of the emergency intercom sent a visceral jolt through his frame. He froze at his stainless-steel workbench, the sterile hum of the equipment warping into the memory of roaring flames. He had withdrawn entirely from field assessments, clinging to the familiar lab to manage the conviction that the world was a dangerous place. His wife noticed the distance hardening around him, how he declined weekend plans to avoid new restaurants or uncharted parking garages. The routine he clung to was fraying. What finally brought Rafael to the clinic was the realization that his avoidance had become a cage. He had missed three major case reviews because he could not bear to leave his known perimeter, and he feared he was losing his professional identity entirely. He sat on the edge of the therapist’s chair, hands clasped tightly, hoping to find a way to quiet the constant readiness in his limbs and to believe, again, that he could navigate a world that no longer felt like a ticking clock.
